## Why multilevel modeling?

-   Let's look at the relationship between SES and math achievement

```{r}

data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/suyoghc/PSY-504_Spring-2025/refs/heads/main/Multilevel%20Modeling/data/heck2011.csv")


```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| 

data_sub <- data %>% 
      filter(schcode <= 10)

data_sub %>% 
      ggplot(mapping = aes(x = ses, y = math)) +
      geom_point2(size=3) +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE) + 
      labs(y="Math Score", x="SES") + 
  theme_lucid(base_size=21)

```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-align: center
#|

tidy() %>%

```

## Why multilevel modeling?

-   However, if we introduce grouping we tell a slightly different story

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

data_sub %>% 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = ses, y = math, colour = factor(schcode))) +
  geom_point2(size=3) +
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(group = schcode), method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE) +
  labs(colour = "schcode") + 
  labs(y="Math Score", x="SES") + 
  ggeasy::easy_add_legend_title("School") + 
    theme_lucid(base_size=21)
```

## What is multilevel modeling?

-   Technique that allows us deal with non-independence between data points (i.e., clustered/nested data)

    -   Nested data violate key assumptions of OLS
        -   ~~independent observations~~
        -   ~~independent errors~~
            -   Biased estimates and/or underestimated SEs, inflating Type 1 error
    -   Correct inferences!

-   Explicit partitioning of the variance

    -   Within (intra-group differences)

    -   Between (inter-group differences)

## What is a "hierarchy?"

> *Clustering = Nesting = Grouping = Hierarchies*

::: {.column width="50%"}

    -   Any complex mixed design

# Simulation: OLS vs. MLM

## OLS vs. MLM

-   We *claimed* that ignoring clusters biases estimates and inflates Type 1 error

-   Let's test this claim with simulated data where we *know* the ground truth, then see which model gets it right

. . .

-   The setup:
    1.  Simulate clustered data where the **true effect of X is zero**
    2.  Fit OLS (ignoring clusters) and MLM (accounting for clusters)
    3.  If OLS finds a "significant" effect, we've caught a Type I error red-handed

## The data generating process

-   30 groups (classrooms, therapists, schools...), 10 observations each
-   Groups differ in their baseline (random intercepts, SD = 3)
-   True slope of `x` is **exactly 0** — there is no effect to find
-   We wrote the equation, so we *know* the truth — can our models recover it?

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(39)
n_groups <- 30; n_per <- 10
group_effects <- rnorm(n_groups, sd = 3)

sim <- tibble(
  group = rep(1:n_groups, each = n_per),
  x = rnorm(n_groups * n_per),
  y = 5 + 0 * x +
      group_effects[group] +
      rnorm(n_groups * n_per)
)
```

```{webr-r}
set.seed(39)                                    # reproducibility
n_groups <- 30; n_per <- 10                     # 30 groups, 10 obs each
group_effects <- rnorm(n_groups, sd = 3)        # random intercepts per group

sim <- tibble(
  group = rep(1:n_groups, each = n_per),        # group labels
  x = rnorm(n_groups * n_per),                  # predictor (continuous)
  y = 5 + 0 * x +                              # true slope is ZERO
      group_effects[group] +                    # between-group variance
      rnorm(n_groups * n_per)                   # within-group variance
)
```

## What does the data look like?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7

sim %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(group))) +
  geom_point2(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Y", x = "X (true effect = 0)",
       title = "OLS sees one big cloud and fits a line through it") +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_lucid(base_size = 21)
```

-   Each color is a different group — notice how groups sit at different heights
-   OLS ignores the group structure. Fits a single line to all 300 points
-   The vertical spread across groups is between-group variance (OLS absorbs it into the error term)

## What happens when we account for groups?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7

sim %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(group))) +
  geom_point2(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = group), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Y", x = "X (true effect = 0)",
       title = "Within each group, there is no relationship") +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_lucid(base_size = 21)
```

-   Within-group lines are mostly flat — exactly what we'd expect when the true slope is zero
-   The OLS line captures **between-group** intercept differences, not the effect of X you're trying to estimate
-   Within each group, the lines are mostly flat — the true slope is zero

## Each group on its own

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8

sim %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(group))) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  labs(y = "Y", x = "X (true effect = 0)") +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme_lucid(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

-   Within-group lines are mostly flat — exactly what we'd expect when the true slope is zero
-   The OLS line captures **between-group** intercept differences, not the effect of X you're trying to estimate
-   Within each group, the lines are mostly flat — the true slope is zero

## OLS vs. MLM: comparing estimates

```{r}
#| echo: false
ols <- lm(y ~ x, data = sim)
mlm <- lmer(y ~ x + (1|group), data = sim)

bind_rows(
  tidy(ols) %>% filter(term == "x") %>% mutate(model = "OLS (ignores clusters)"),
  tidy(mlm) %>% filter(term == "x") %>% mutate(model = "MLM (accounts for clusters)")
) %>%
  select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{webr-r}
ols <- lm(y ~ x, data = sim)
mlm <- lmer(y ~ x + (1|group), data = sim)

bind_rows(
  tidy(ols) %>% filter(term == "x") %>% mutate(model = "OLS (ignores clusters)"),
  tidy(mlm) %>% filter(term == "x") %>% mutate(model = "MLM (accounts for clusters)")
) %>%
  select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

. . .

::: callout-important
-   The true effect is **zero** — but OLS finds *p* = .016!
-   If this were a real study, we'd publish a false finding
-   MLM correctly concludes no effect (*p* = .91)
-   The OLS estimate (-0.32) is far from zero because between-group variance contaminates it. MLM's estimate (-0.006) recovers the truth
:::

## What went wrong with OLS?

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   OLS sees 300 "independent" observations

-   Between-group differences in Y get **absorbed into the residuals**

-   This contaminates the slope estimate, pulling it away from the true value

-   Biased estimate $\rightarrow$ false significance
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   MLM **partitions** the variance:

    -   Between-group variance: $\sigma^2_{U_0}$
    -   Within-group variance: $\sigma^2_e$

-   The slope is estimated using only **within-group** variation

-   Unbiased estimate $\rightarrow$ correct conclusion
:::
:::

## The equations: one error vs. many

-   OLS has **one** error term — everything unexplained goes into a single pile:

$$y_i = \color{blue}{b_0 + b_1 x_i} + \color{red}{e_i}$$

-   MLM splits that pile into **separate sources** of variance:

$$y_{ij} = \color{blue}{\gamma_0 + \gamma_1 x_{ij}} + \color{red}{U_{0j}} + \color{red}{e_{ij}}$$

-   $\color{red}{U_{0j}}$ = how far group $j$'s intercept deviates from the grand mean (between-group error)
-   $\color{red}{e_{ij}}$ = how far observation $i$ deviates from its group mean (within-group error)

## Mapping the equation to our simulation code

-   Our data generating process **is** the MLM equation:

```
y = 5 + 0 * x + group_effects[group] + rnorm(...)
```

| Code                    | Equation          | What it is                |
|-------------------------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| `5`                     | $\gamma_0$        | Fixed intercept           |
| `0 * x`                | $\gamma_1 x_{ij}$ | Fixed slope (set to zero) |
| `group_effects[group]` | $U_{0j}$          | Between-group error       |
| `rnorm(...)`           | $e_{ij}$          | Within-group error        |

-   OLS lumps $U_{0j}$ and $e_{ij}$ into one $e_i$ — it can't tell them apart
-   MLM recovers both, so the slope estimate reflects only the within-group relationship

## Reading the code

-   OLS: `lm(y ~ x)` — one equation, one error term, all observations treated as independent
-   MLM: `lmer(y ~ x + (1|group))` — same fixed effect, but `(1|group)` lets each group have its own intercept
-   That one addition is what partitioned the variance, gave us an unbiased estimate, and prevented the false positive
-   We'll unpack the full `lmer` syntax later

. . .

-   Now let's see this in action with an interactive simulation

# In-Class Exercise

## Interactive Simulation App

Open the simulation app on your laptop:

[**Launch the MLM Simulation App**](https://j4ei32-suyog-chandramouli.shinyapps.io/mlm-simulation/){target="_blank"}

Use the sliders to control:

- **Between-group SD** — how strong the clustering is
- **True slope** — the real effect of X on Y
- **Number of groups** and **observations per group**
- Hit **Re-simulate** for a new random draw

## Questions

**Q1: Set between-group SD = 0, true slope = 0.** Compare OLS and MLM. What do you notice? What is the ICC?

<br>

**Q2: Keep true slope = 0, increase between-group SD to 3.** What happens to the OLS p-value? What about MLM? Look at the plots. Why does OLS find a significant effect?

<br>

**Q3: Set true slope = 0.5, between-group SD = 3.** Compare the OLS and MLM estimates. Which is closer to 0.5?

<br>

**Q4: Set true slope = 0. Slowly decrease between-group SD from 3 → 2 → 1 → 0.5 → 0.** At what ICC do OLS and MLM start agreeing?

## Q1: Baseline

**Set between-group SD = 0, true slope = 0.** Compare OLS and MLM. What do you notice? What is the ICC?

## A1: Baseline

- OLS and MLM give essentially **identical** results
- Both correctly find no significant effect
- ICC ≈ 0, no variance is between groups
- **Takeaway:** when there's no clustering, OLS is fine and MLM adds nothing

## Q2: Introduce clustering

**Keep true slope = 0, increase between-group SD to 3.** What happens to the OLS p-value? What about MLM? Look at the plots. Why does OLS find a significant effect?

## A2: Introduce clustering

- OLS often finds p < .05, a **false positive** (the true effect is zero!)
- MLM correctly finds no significant effect
- The plots show groups sitting at different heights, which OLS cannot distinguish from a real effect
- Within each group, the lines are flat, there's no real relationship
- ICC jumps to ~0.90, most variance is between groups

## Q3: A real effect

**Set true slope = 0.5, between-group SD = 3.** Compare the OLS and MLM estimates. Which is closer to 0.5?

## A3: A real effect

- MLM consistently estimates close to **0.5** (the true value)
- OLS is more variable, often overshooting or undershooting
- Between-group variance contaminates the OLS estimate even when there IS a real effect
- MLM isolates the within-group relationship, which is where the true effect lives

## Q4: The threshold

**Set true slope = 0. Slowly decrease between-group SD from 3 → 2 → 1 → 0.5 → 0.** Watch the ICC and model table. At what point do OLS and MLM start agreeing?

## A4: The threshold

- Around **ICC ≈ 0.20 or below** (between-group SD around 0.5–1), OLS and MLM converge
- When clustering is weak, OLS is approximately fine
- When clustering is strong, you **need** MLM
- The ICC is your diagnostic: it tells you how much the grouping structure matters

# Multilevel models are awesome!

## Why MLM is Awesome

-   Classic analysis:

    -   Aggregate to level of the group (e.g., with means)

-   Drawback of classic analysis:

    -   Loss of resolution!
    -   Loss of power!

-   MLM Approach:

    -   Deaggregation (keep all the data)

## Why MLM is Awesome

-   Classic Analysis:

    -   Repeated-measures ANOVA

-   Drawback of this approach:

    -   Missing data

        -   Must exclude entire people OR, you can interpolate missing data

-   MLM Approach:

    -   Can analyze all the observations you have!

## Why MLM is Awesome

-   Classic Analysis:

    -   Repeated-measures ANOVA

-   Drawback of ANOVA:

    -   Only use categorical predictors

-   MLM Approach:

    -   Can use any combo of categorical and continuous predictors!

## Why MLM is Awesome

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   ***Interdependence***
    -   You can model the relationships between cases (regression for repeated observations)
-   ***Missing data***
    -   Uses ML for missing data
-   ***Power***
    -   Deaggregated data
-   ***Take into account within and between variance***
-   ***Flexibility***
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/lego.webp){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::::

## Multilevel models

-   When to use them:

    -   Nested designs

    -   Repeated measures

    -   Longitudinal data

    -   Complex designs

-   Why use them:

    -   Captures variance occurring between groups and within groups

-   What they are:

    -   Linear model with extra residuals

## Why not use MLM?

-   Dont really care about variance (it is just a nuisance variable)

    -   Use GEEs (generalized estimating equations)
    -   Clustered standard errors

-   Data is not actually interdependent

    -   Test with ICC

-   Small number of groups/clusters

-   You only have a between-subjects design

# Important Terminology

## Jumping right in

-   Words you hear constantly in MLM Land:

    -   *Fixed effects*
    -   *Random effects*
    -   *Random factors*
    -   *Random intercepts*
    -   *Random slopes*

-   What do they all mean?

## Fixed and random effects

-   Two sides to any model

    $$
    y_i = \color{blue}{b_{0_{\text{(intercept)}}} + b_{1_{\text{(slope)}}} x_i} + e_{i_{\text{(error)}}}
    $$

    -   Model for the means (fixed part):

        -   **Fixed effect (constant effect)**:

            -   Population-level (i.e., average) effects that should persist across clusters/experiments

::: callout-note
-   What you are used to caring about for testing hypotheses

<!-- -->

-   Our predictor variables (can be continuous or categorical)
:::

## Fixed and random effects

-   Model for the variance (random part):

$$
y_i = {b_{0_{\text{(intercept)}}} + b_{1_{\text{(slope)}}} x_i} + \color{red}{e_{i_{\text{(error)}}}}
$$

-   Uncorrelated with fixed part

-   Variation around the expected values

-   Normal distributed \~ $N(\mu,\sigma)$

. . .

-   In MLM multiple "piles of variance" or residual terms

## Random factors and random effects

-   Random factors:

    -   Represent higher level grouping variables

        -   A random sample of an infinite number of possible levels

<!-- -->

-   ::: callout-note
    Can only be categorical!
    :::

## Random factors vs random effects

-   The random factor is your clustering variable:

    -   Participants 🧑‍🤝‍🧑

    -   Schools 🏫

    -   Words

    -   Pictures 🖼️

## Random factors vs random effects

-   Random effects:

    -   How random factors are allowed to vary

        -   Random intercept (most common) : $U_{0j}$

            -   Each level-2 cluster has its own average level-1 outcome

        -   Random slope: $U_{1j}$

            -   Each level-2 cluster has its own coef for the effect of a predictor on the outcome

                -   **You have a choice about whether or not to allow your Level 1 intercept and slopes to have variability**

## Is it a random or fixed factor?

-   Should my variable be fixed or random?

    -   If it is continuous, has few levels (\<5), or is an experimental manipulation

        -   Fixed

-   Want to estimate variance at each level of factor?

    -   Fixed

-   Want a general estimate of variance of factor?

    -   Random

## What is random and what is fixed?

-   **Scenario**: Investigating how student performance is influenced by teaching methods and individual student characteristics across different schools.

    -   **Data Collected**: student socio-economic status (SES), teaching method used (e.g., traditional, modern), and school ID

        -   What is fixed?

        -   What is random?

# Specifiying MLMs

## Single-level (fixed) regression

-   Blue = fixed

-   Red = random

    $$y_i = \color{blue}{b_{0_{\text{(intercept)}}} + b_{1_{\text{(slope)}}} x_i} + \color{red}{ e_{i_{\text{(error)}}}}$$

$$
e_{i_{\text{(error)}}} = y_i - \hat{y}_i
$$

![](images/null5.png){fig-align="center"}

## Random intercept

-   Varying starting point per higher level/group variable

$$
y_{ij} = (\color{blue}{b_{0j_{\text{(intercept)}}}} + \color{red}{U_{0j_{\text{(random intercept)}}}}) + \color{blue}{b_{1_{\text{(slope)}}} x_{ij}} + \color{red}{e_{ij_{\text{(error)}}}}
$$

$$
U_{0j} = b_{0j} - b_0
$$

-   Between-group variation

![](images/ranint3.png){fig-align="center"}

i = individual observation j = group

## Random intercepts

$$
y_{ij} = ({b_{0j_{\text{(intercept)}}} + U_{0j_{\text{(random intercept)}}}}) + b_{1_{\text{(slope)}}} x_{ij} + \color{red}{ e_{ij_{\text{(error)}}}}
$$

Within-group variation

![](images/ranint2.png){fig-align="center" width="491"}

## Random intercepts - fixed slope

-   Varying starting point (intercept), same slope for each group

![](images/ranint.png){fig-align="center"}

## Random Intercepts - Random slopes

-   Varying starting point (intercept), varying slope for each group

$$
y_{ij} = (\color{blue}{b_{0j_{\text{(intercept)}}}} + \color{red}{U_{0j_{\text{(random intercept)}}}}) + (\color{blue}{b_{1_{\text{(slope)}}} x_{ij}} + \color{red}{U_{1j_{\text{(random slope)}}}}) +  \color{red}{e_{ij_{\text{(error)}}}}
$$

::: callout-important
-   ***Only put a random slope if it changes within cluster/group***
:::

![](images/ranintslope.png){fig-align="center"}

## Random slopes

-   The dotted lines are fixed slopes. The arrows show the added error term for each random slope

$$
U_{1j} = b_{1j} - b_1
$$

![](images/randintslope3.png){fig-align="center"}

## MLM Equations

+-----------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **Level** | **Equation**                                                                |
+===========+=============================================================================+
| Level 1   | $y_{ij} = b_{0j} + b_{1j}X_{ij} + e_{ij}$                                   |
+-----------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Level 2   | $b_{0j}=γ00+U_{0j}$                                                         |
|           |                                                                             |
|           | $b_{1j} = \gamma{10} + U_{1j}$                                              |
+-----------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Combined  | $y_{ij} = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}X_{ij} + e_{ij} + U_{b0j} + U_{b1j}X_{ij}$ |
+-----------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

-   You will see both equations used in the literature

## All together

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](https://bookdown.org/steve_midway/DAR/images/07_models.png){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Fit models using `lmer` in `lme4` package

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| 
lm(math~ses, data=data) # lm

lmer(math~ses + (1|schcode), data=data) # random intercept fixed slope

lmer(math~ses + (0+ ses |schcode), data=data) # random slope fixed intercept

lmer(math~ses + (1+ses|schcode), data=data) # random intercept + random slope
```
:::
:::::

## Syntax cheat sheet

![](images/lmesyntax.png){fig-align="center"}

## How do your groups differ?

-   Different averages

    -   **Random intercept**

        -   Each group gets its own intercept

-   Different relationships between x and y

    -   **Random Slope**

        -   Each group gets its own slope

## Implications

-   Multiple sources of variance?

    -   Just add more residuals!

-   Each source of variance gets its own residual term

    -   Residuals capture variance

    -   Residuals are added rendering them conditionally independent

        -   Otherwise, MLM is the same as GLM

## How are MLMs similar to LM?

-   The fixed effects (usually) hold your hypothesis tests

    -   Fixed effects output: Looks like GLM output

-   Can (essentially) be interpreted like GLM output

-   For most people, this is all that matters

## How are LM and MLM different?

-   MLM has random effects output

    -   Variance explained by the random effect

    -   This may be interesting, in and of itself

-   Fixed effects of random terms are the average estimates across groups
